teaser: A halo, a holy title, and a woman no church would hang.
review_notes:
Image appears consistent with the Munch Museum version (signed lower left); several painted versions exist (c. 1894-95), check the count of five.
Alternative titles 'Loving Woman' and 'Conception'.
Munch's text about the moment of conception and 'a corpse's smile' is paraphrased.
Dagny Juel as model is a common but unproven identification; her death in Tbilisi in 1901.
Lithograph (1895) border with sperm cells and fetus; lost painted frame reported for an early version.
2004 theft: 22 August, armed robbers, Munch Museum; both works recovered 31 August 2006; Madonna suffered tears/holes in the canvas: check details.
Dimensions about 90 x 68.5 cm.

lesson.text: The title says Madonna: the Virgin Mary, the most painted holy woman in Western art. The picture says something else. She is naked to the hips, eyes closed, head thrown back, and nothing about her is praying. Edvard Munch put the two together in 1894 and left them to fight.

He knew exactly which rules he was breaking. For five hundred years a Madonna had meant a clothed young mother, eyes lowered, usually holding her child, with a gold ring of light around her head. Munch keeps one of those ingredients, and only one.

spots.title: The halo
spots.text: Not gold but red, the color of blood and desire, and tilted like a beret. It is the only thing in the picture that still says “saint.”

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Eyelids shut and shadowed, lips parted. The pale mask with dark hollows around the eyes looks ecstatic and, at the same time, a little like a skull.

spots.title: The vanishing arm
spots.text: One arm bends up behind her head and fades into the dark. The other disappears behind her back. With no hands to push us away or cover herself, she is completely given over.

lesson.text: That skull-like shadow in the face is not an accident. Munch wrote about this image as the instant a new life is conceived, when a woman becomes one link in a chain running from the dead to the unborn. Love, birth and death in one body: that is his idea of holiness.

Munch did not always call her Madonna. The same image was also exhibited under the titles “Loving Woman” and “Conception.” He painted it several times in about two years, and the versions hang today in Oslo, Hamburg and private collections.

Look at what surrounds her. There is no room, no bed, no horizon. Bands of dark red, blue and brown curve around the body as if she were floating in water, or as if she gave off waves. The paint is so thin that the weave of the canvas shows through, and Munch let it run.

Are we standing in front of her, or lying beneath her? Many viewers feel the second. The picture puts you in the place of her lover, and that, more than the nudity, is what shocked people in the 1890s.

In 1895 Munch turned the image into a lithograph, a print drawn on stone. Around it he added a border of swimming sperm cells and, in the bottom corner, a tiny, sad-eyed fetus. An early painted version is said to have had a carved frame with the same motifs, now lost.

Who was she? Friends of Munch pointed to Dagny Juel, a Norwegian writer at the center of his circle of artists in Berlin, admired by several of the men in it. Munch never confirmed it. He was after a type, not a likeness: woman as he both worshipped and feared her.

On August 22, 2004, masked men with guns walked into the Munch Museum in Oslo in broad daylight and tore this Madonna and a version of The Scream off the wall. Both were missing for two years. They came back in 2006, the Madonna with tears in its canvas that restorers had to mend.
Munch did not paint the Virgin Mary and he did not simply paint a nude. He borrowed a sacred name to say that the most ordinary human act, making a new life, deserves a halo.
Wander over the surface yourself. Knowing the canvas was ripped from a wall and hidden for two years, its thin, fragile skin of paint is worth a slow look.

spots.title: Red halo
spots.text: A thick arc of scarlet, the strongest color on the canvas, set against black hair.

spots.title: Closed eyes
spots.text: Greenish shadows ring the eye sockets. Pleasure and a death mask in the same face.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: Black hair streams down over her shoulder in separate wavy strands and melts into the background currents.

spots.title: The belly
spots.text: A warm, softly modeled stomach with a red touch at the navel: the place where, in Munch's mind, the chain of generations continues.

spots.title: The aura
spots.text: Curved bands of blue and ocher wrap around her like ripples. They repeat the outline of the body outward.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: “E Munch” in red, the halo's color, in the bottom corner.

quiz.question: What color is the halo in Munch's Madonna?
quiz.explanation: Munch replaced the traditional gold ring with a red one.

quiz.question: What moment did Munch say the picture is about?
options: The conception of a new life
A dancer resting after a show
quiz.explanation: He wrote of the instant when a woman becomes a link between the dead and the unborn.

quiz.question: What did Munch add around the lithograph version?
options: A border of sperm cells and a small fetus
quiz.explanation: The print's border makes the theme of conception explicit.

quiz.question: What happened to this painting in 2004?
options: It was stolen at gunpoint from the Munch Museum
It was discovered in an attic
quiz.explanation: It was taken together with a version of The Scream and recovered in 2006.

quiz.question: What happens to the woman's arms?
options: They fade away behind her head and back
quiz.explanation: With no visible hands she neither covers herself nor pushes the viewer away.

facts.text: Munch painted only one version of Madonna.
facts.explanation: He painted it several times and also made a lithograph.

facts.text: The picture was also shown under the title “Loving Woman.”
facts.explanation: Munch used several titles, including “Loving Woman” and “Conception.”

facts.text: The woman sits in a carefully described bedroom.
facts.explanation: There is no setting at all, only curved bands of thin color around her body.
